variants.title: EJ20 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: "EJ20" is a family name covering dozens of distinct variants across 25+ years of production. The differences matter enormously - a naturally aspirated EJ20E is not a straight swap for a turbocharged EJ205, and even within the same sub-code there are revision differences. ### EJ20E - 1989-2011 (SOHC, naturally aspirated) - Fitted to: Subaru Impreza (base models), Legacy (base models), Forester (base models) - Key technical difference: Single overhead camshaft (SOHC), 16-valve. European spec: 115 hp; Japanese spec: 125-155 hp depending on compression ratio. No AVCS. Hydraulic lifters on early versions (pre-1994). - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family patterns - cylinder 4 knock at high mileage, oil leaks from camshaft seals. Generally the most reliable EJ20 variant. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with DOHC variants - cam covers, timing belt arrangement, and ECU differ significantly. ### EJ201 - 1998-2005 (SOHC, naturally aspirated) - Fitted to: Subaru Impreza, Legacy, Forester - Key technical difference: SOHC, 16-valve. Two power outputs: 125 hp or 135 hp. No hydraulic lifters. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family patterns. - Interchange note: Generally interchangeable with EJ202 but check ECU compatibility. ### EJ202 - 1998-2009 (SOHC, naturally aspirated) - Fitted to: Subaru Legacy, Forester - Key technical difference: SOHC, 16-valve. 130-140 hp. Received a lightweight cylinder block in 2003. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family patterns. - Interchange note: 2003+ lightweight block variants are not a direct swap with earlier EJ202s without checking engine mounts and sump configuration. ### EJ203 - 2002-2009 (SOHC, naturally aspirated, electronic throttle) - Fitted to: Subaru Forester (second generation), Legacy (fourth generation) - Key technical difference: SOHC, 16-valve. 140 hp. Features electronic throttle (drive-by-wire) - the first EJ20 variant to use it. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Electronic throttle can cause idle fluctuations and hesitation. Shares the family mechanical failure patterns. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with cable-throttle EJ20s - ECU, throttle body, and wiring loom are completely different. ### EJ204 - 1999-2015 (DOHC, naturally aspirated, AVCS) - Fitted to: Subaru Impreza, Legacy, Forester - Key technical difference: Dual overhead camshaft (DOHC), 16-valve. 150-190 hp depending on tune. Features Subaru's AVCS (Active Valve Control System) variable valve timing. Higher compression ratio (10-11:1). Slightly heavier than other EJ20 variants (120 kg vs 110 kg). - Sub-code-specific failure note: AVCS system can suffer from oil pressure issues and solenoid failures. Shares the family mechanical failure patterns. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with non-AVCS EJ20s - requires AVCS-compatible ECU and wiring. ### EJ20G / EJ20K / EJ205 / EJ207 - Turbocharged variants (1990s-2000s) - Fitted to: Subaru Impreza WRX, STI, Legacy GT, Forester XT - Key technical difference: Turbocharged, DOHC, closed-deck block on early versions (EJ20G), later open-deck. EJ20G: 200-220 hp, first to use oil squirters and low-compression pistons. EJ20K: revised heads, higher output. EJ205: single AVCS, 225-250 hp (UK WRX 1998-2005). EJ207: twin-scroll turbo, 280 hp (JDM STI). - Sub-code-specific failure note: Turbocharged EJ20s suffer the same failures as NA variants but at higher rates - cylinder 4 knock is more common due to higher cylinder pressures; oil consumption is significantly worse. - Interchange note: These are not interchangeable without the correct ECU, wiring loom, turbo, and intercooler. An EJ207 is not a drop-in replacement for an EJ205. ### EJ20X / EJ20Y - 2005-2015 (Turbo, JDM Legacy) - Fitted to: Subaru Legacy GT (JDM), Subaru Outback XT (JDM) - Key technical difference: Turbocharged, DOHC, 92.0mm bore, 75.0mm stroke. 280 hp (EJ20Y) and 260 hp (EJ20X) depending on tune. Single AVCS. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family patterns. The EJ20Y is particularly prone to turbocharger oil starvation. - Interchange note: JDM-spec engines require ECU reflash and may need different fuel mapping for UK fuel quality.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement EJ20 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used EJ20 makes sense only if it comes with documented evidence of timing belt replacement (within the last 5 years/60k miles) and no history of overheating. Naturally aspirated EJ20s (EJ20E, EJ201, EJ202) are generally safe used purchases if the mileage is under 100k - these are robust engines. Turbocharged EJ20s (EJ205, EJ207) are high-risk used purchases - cylinder 4 knock and oil consumption are common, and many have been modified and abused.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper EJ20 recon addresses the known weak points: new timing belt kit (tensioner, idlers, water pump), new head gaskets (MLS), new camshaft seals and valve cover gaskets, and - for turbo variants - a turbocharger inspection and new oil feed lines. Naturally aspirated recons typically cost £1,200-£1,800; turbo recons £1,800-£2,500. A 12-month warranty is standard. This is the sweet spot for most UK owners.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full EJ20 rebuild is justified when you want to keep a specific vehicle (e.g. a clean Impreza WRX or early Legacy GT) and want the engine to last another 150,000+ miles. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons (especially important for turbo variants to prevent cylinder 4 knock), ARP head studs, new oil pump, and a fully reconditioned cylinder head with new valve guides and seals. Budget £2,000-£3,500 for a quality rebuild.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All of our vetted UK Subaru specialists offer supply-only or full supply-and-fit - nationwide delivery and recovery available, with warranties that cover both parts and labour.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The EJ20 sits across a wide value range - early Impreza and Legacy values range from £1,000-£5,000; later examples £3,000-£10,000; WRX and STI variants command £5,000-£15,000+ depending on condition. A reconditioned EJ20 at £1,200-£2,500 represents 15-50% of vehicle value - generally viable for most examples. However, for a high-mileage (£1,000-£2,000) base Impreza or Legacy, a full rebuild at £3,500 may exceed the vehicle's value. In those cases, evaluate the car's overall condition, rust, and interior before committing. For naturally aspirated cars, a used engine with documented history is often the most economical route .

items.question: How much does a Subaru EJ20 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned EJ20 supply-only costs £1,200-£2,500, with fitted prices from £2,100-£3,400. Used units start from £800 supply-only. Rebuilt engines with upgraded internals cost £2,000-£3,500 supply-only.
bullets: Rebuilt engines with upgraded internals cost £2,000-£3,500 supply‑only.

items.question: What are the most common EJ20 engine problems?
items.answer: The EJ20 suffers from cylinder 4 piston knock (high mileage), oil consumption and leaks (especially turbocharged variants), and timing belt failure if the 100,000 km / 5-year service is missed. Timing belt replacement costs £400-£800. Head gasket replacement £800-£1,500. Cylinder 4 knock repair often requires a full rebuild.
bullets: Cylinder 4 knock repair often requires a full rebuild.

items.question: Which Subaru models use the EJ20 engine?
items.answer: The EJ20 was fitted to the Subaru Impreza (1992-2012), Legacy (1989-2012), Forester (1997-2011), Outback (1995-2009), and Baja (2003-2006). Check your model’s compatibility
bullets: The Impreza is the highest‑volume application in the UK.
Naturally aspirated EJ20s are more common than turbos.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned EJ20?
items.answer: A reconditioned EJ20 is the safer choice - it includes a new timing belt, new gaskets, and a 12-month warranty. Used NA EJ20s with documented service history can be a good value. Used turbo EJ20s are high-risk without full history.
bullets: Used NA EJ20s with documented service history can be a good value.
Used turbo EJ20s are high‑risk without full history.

items.question: What’s the difference between EJ20 and EJ25?
items.answer: The EJ25 is a 2.5‑litre engine (vs 2.0‑litre) with more torque and power, but also higher head‑gasket failure rates. See the EJ25 page for details
bullets: The EJ20 is generally more reliable and cheaper to replace.
The EJ25 is not a direct drop‑in replacement without ECU and wiring changes.

items.question: How long does an EJ20 engine last?
items.answer: With regular maintenance (timing belt every 100,000 km / 5 years, oil changes every 5k-6k miles), an EJ20 can exceed 200,000 miles - especially the naturally aspirated versions. Turbocharged variants typically last 150,000 miles with careful use. Cylinder 4 knock is the main limit on high-mileage units.
